content: The antisecretory effect of pantoprazole persists for more than 24 hours across all tested doses, ranging from 20 mg to 120 mg. The active ingredient in pantoprazole sodium delayed-release tablets, USP, is a substituted benzimidazole compound known as sodium 5-(difluoromethoxy)-2-(((3,4-dimethoxy-2-pyridinyl)methyl)sulfinyl)-1H-benzimidazole sesquihydrate. This compound functions as an inhibitor of gastric acid secretion. Pantoprazole sodium sesquihydrate is a white to off-white crystalline powder that is racemic in nature. It exhibits weakly basic and acidic properties and is practically insoluble in n-hexane. The stability of pantoprazole in aqueous solution is pH-dependent, with the rate of degradation increasing as the pH decreases. Pantoprazole sodium is available as delayed-release tablets in two strengths: 20 mg and 40 mg. Each tablet contains 55 mg of pantoprazole sodium sesquihydrate, USP, equivalent to either 20 mg or 40 mg of pantoprazole, respectively. The tablets also include inactive ingredients such as calcium stearate, crospovidone, hydroxypropyl cellulose, hypromellose, mannitol, methacrylic acid copolymer dispersion, propylene glycol, sodium carbonate, talc, titanium dioxide, and triethyl citrate. These tablets meet the USP Dissolution Test 3 standards. Under maximal acid stimulatory conditions induced by pentagastrin, pantoprazole demonstrates a dose-dependent reduction in gastric acid output following a single oral dose (20–80 mg) or a single intravenous dose (20–120 mg) in healthy volunteers. Daily administration of pantoprazole results in progressive inhibition of gastric acid secretion, with a mean inhibition of 85% achieved after 7 days of once-daily dosing. In more than half of the subjects, acid secretion was suppressed by over 95%. Gastric acid secretion returned to normal within one week after the final dose, with no evidence of rebound hypersecretion. In dose-response studies, oral doses of pantoprazole ranging from 20 mg to 120 mg produced dose-related increases in median basal gastric pH and the percentage of time gastric pH remained above 3 and 4. A 40 mg dose of pantoprazole resulted in significantly greater increases in gastric pH compared to the 20 mg dose. However, doses higher than 40 mg (e.g., 60 mg, 80 mg, 120 mg) did not produce further significant increases in median gastric pH. Fasting serum gastrin levels were evaluated in two double-blind studies involving 682 patients with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) undergoing treatment for erosive esophagitis (EE). Patients received 10 mg, 20 mg, or 40 mg of pantoprazole for up to 8 weeks. After 4 weeks of treatment, mean serum gastrin levels increased by 7%, 35%, and 72% over pretreatment values in the 10 mg, 20 mg, and 40 mg groups, respectively. At 8 weeks, mean increases were 3%, 26%, and 84% for the respective dose groups. Median serum gastrin levels remained within normal limits during maintenance therapy with pantoprazole sodium delayed-release tablets. In long-term international studies involving over 800 patients, a 2to 3-fold increase in fasting serum gastrin levels was observed during the initial months of treatment with pantoprazole at doses of 40 mg per day for GERD maintenance therapy or 40 mg or higher per day in patients with refractory GERD. These elevated gastrin levels generally stabilized at approximately 2 to 3 times baseline levels for up to 4 years of periodic follow-up in clinical trials. Following short-term treatment with pantoprazole, elevated gastrin levels returned to normal within approximately 3 months. In 39 patients treated with oral pantoprazole at doses ranging from 40 mg to 240 mg daily (most receiving 40 mg to 80 mg) for up to 5 years, a moderate increase in enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cell density was observed, beginning after the first year of use and appearing to plateau after 4 years. In animal studies, pantoprazole administered at doses of 5 to 200 mg/kg/day resulted in dose-related increases in gastric ECL cell proliferation and gastric neuroendocrine (NE) cell tumors. The development of gastric NE cell tumors in rats may be attributed to chronic elevation of serum gastrin concentrations.
